- **[PyTorch Segmented Polynomial Module](12-pytorch-segmented-polynomial-module)** — Deep dive into the `SegmentedPolynomial` PyTorch wrapper, including the `uniform_1d` vs `naive` method distinction and `input_indices` mechanics.
- **[Rotation and Symmetric Contraction](11-rotation-and-symmetric-contraction)** — Explore the mathematical foundations of symmetric contractions and their relationship to rotation descriptors.
- **[Model Examples: MACE and NequIP](21-model-examples-mace-and-nequip)** — See how `SymmetricContraction` integrates into full equivariant architectures like MACE.

# Tensor Product Operations



Tensor product operations form the computational backbone of any equivariant neural network — they are the mechanism by which geometric information propagates while respecting rotational symmetry. In cuEquivariance's PyTorch backend, these operations are implemented as `torch.nn.Module` subclasses that internally leverage the **descriptor system** to define their polynomial structure and the **SegmentedPolynomial** engine to execute the computation. This page covers the three core operation classes, the composite message-passing convolution layer, and the shared architectural patterns that unify them all.

## Operation Landscape

The PyTorch operations module at `cuequivariance_torch/operations/` provides a layered hierarchy of equivariant building blocks. Each class follows a consistent design: it obtains a descriptor from the `cuequivariance.descriptors` API, sets up layout transposition layers to convert between user-facing and internal irreps layouts, and delegates the actual computation to `SegmentedPolynomial` with a chosen execution method.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class TPBase {
        <<torch.nn.Module>>
        +shared_weights: bool
        +internal_weights: bool
        +weight_numel: int
        +method: str
        +transpose_in/out: TransposeIrrepsLayout
        +f: SegmentedPolynomial
    }

    class Linear {
        +irreps_in: Irreps
        +irreps_out: Irreps
        +weight_classes: int
        +forward(x, weight, weight_indices) Tensor
    }

    class FullyConnectedTensorProduct {
        +irreps_in1: Irreps
        +irreps_in2: Irreps
        +irreps_out: Irreps
        +forward(x1, x2, weight) Tensor
    }

    class ChannelWiseTensorProduct {
        +irreps_in1: Irreps
        +irreps_in2: Irreps
        +irreps_out: Irreps
        +forward(x1, x2, weight, indices...) Tensor
    }

    class FullyConnectedTensorProductConv {
        +in_irreps: Irreps
        +sh_irreps: Irreps
        +out_irreps: Irreps
        +tp: FullyConnectedTensorProduct
        +mlp: Sequential
        +batch_norm: BatchNorm
        +forward(src_features, edge_sh, edge_emb, graph, ...) Tensor
    }

    TPBase <|-- Linear
    TPBase <|-- FullyConnectedTensorProduct
    TPBase <|-- ChannelWiseTensorProduct
    FullyConnectedTensorProductConv --> FullyConnectedTensorProduct : composes
```

The three core operations differ in how they couple input irreps to output irreps, which directly determines their mathematical structure, weight tensor shapes, and applicable CUDA kernels.

Sources: [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L30-L31), [tp_channel_wise.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_channel_wise.py#L30-L31), [linear.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/linear.py#L30-L31)

## Mathematical Structure and Descriptor Subscripts

Every tensor product operation is defined by its **Einstein subscript notation**, which specifies exactly how operands are contracted. Understanding these subscripts is the key to choosing the right operation for your architecture.

**FullyConnectedTensorProduct** uses the subscript `"uvw,iu,jv,kw+ijk"` [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L106). Here, three input operands — weight (`u,v,w`), first feature (`i,u`), and second feature (`j,v`) — are contracted through shared indices to produce the output (`i,j,k`). Each path from input to output has its own independent weight, giving maximum expressivity: every valid Clebsch-Gordan coupling path between `irreps_in1`, `irreps_in2`, and `irreps_out` receives a separate learnable scalar.

**ChannelWiseTensorProduct** uses `"uv,iu,jv,kuv+ijk"` [tp_channel_wise.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_channel_wise.py#L110). The critical difference is that the weight operand shares the `u,v` indices with the inputs rather than having an independent `w` dimension. This means the weight tensor has a coupled structure — the number of weight parameters equals the number of valid coupling paths, not the full Cartesian product. This makes the channel-wise variant more parameter-efficient when output irreps are filtered or constrained.

**Linear** reduces the problem to a single operand with subscript `"uv,iu,iv"` [linear.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/linear.py#L92). The weight `u,v` maps input irreps `i,u` directly to output irreps `i,v` without mixing different irrep degrees — this is the equivariant analog of a standard linear layer, preserving the irrep degree of each channel.

| Operation | Subscript | Inputs | Weight Coupling | Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `FullyConnectedTensorProduct` | `uvw,iu,jv,kw+ijk` | Two feature tensors | Fully independent per path | NequIP-style message passing |
| `ChannelWiseTensorProduct` | `uv,iu,jv,kuv+ijk` | Two feature tensors | Coupled to input degrees | MACE, PaiNN |
| `Linear` | `uv,iu,iv` | One feature tensor | Per-degree mixing | Irrep mixing, equivariant MLP |

Sources: [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L106), [tp_channel_wise.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_channel_wise.py#L110), [linear.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/linear.py#L92)

## FullyConnectedTensorProduct

The `FullyConnectedTensorProduct` is the most general form of equivariant bilinear operation. It takes two input tensors of arbitrary irreps, couples them through all valid Clebsch-Gordan paths, and produces output features whose irreps are user-specified. This operation is the direct counterpart to `e3nn.nn.FullyConnectedTensorProduct`, with the key difference that cuEquivariance defaults to the `"fused_tp"` CUDA kernel for maximum throughput.

### Constructor and Configuration

The constructor accepts two input irreps and one output irreps, plus a family of layout and execution parameters [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L58-L75):

```python
tp = cuet.FullyConnectedTensorProduct(
    irreps_in1="4x0e + 4x1o",
    irreps_in2="0e + 1o",
    irreps_out="4x0e + 4x1o",
    layout=cue.mul_ir,       # e3nn-compatible layout
    shared_weights=True,      # share weights across batch
    internal_weights=True,    # create nn.Parameter internally
    method="fused_tp",        # CUDA kernel (default)
    math_dtype=torch.float32, # precision for computation
)
```

The `method` parameter controls which execution backend is used. When set to `"fused_tp"` (the default when CUDA is available), a custom fused CUDA kernel handles the entire segmented tensor product in a single launch. The deprecated `use_fallback=True` maps to `method="naive"`, which uses a pure PyTorch implementation based on scatter/gather operations [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L128-L141).

### Weight Modes

The operation supports two weight management patterns. With `internal_weights=True` (the default when `shared_weights=True`), the module creates a `torch.nn.Parameter` of shape `(1, weight_numel)` and manages it internally. With `internal_weights=False`, the user must supply weights at forward time, enabling scenarios where weights are computed dynamically by a separate network [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L117-L127):

```python
# Internal weights — simplest usage
tp = cuet.FullyConnectedTensorProduct(irreps_in1, irreps_in2, irreps_out)
output = tp(x1, x2)

# External weights — for dynamic weight generation
tp = cuet.FullyConnectedTensorProduct(irreps_in1, irreps_in2, irreps_out, internal_weights=False)
weights = mlp(edge_embeddings)  # shape: (num_edges, weight_numel)
output = tp(x1_per_edge, x2_per_edge, weight=weights)
```

> [!TIP]
> When using `shared_weights=False` with external weights, the weight tensor must have shape `(batch_size, weight_numel)` — each element in the batch gets its own set of path weights. This is the pattern used inside `FullyConnectedTensorProductConv` where per-edge weights are generated by an MLP.

Sources: [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L58-L141), [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L166-L207)

## ChannelWiseTensorProduct

The `ChannelWiseTensorProduct` imposes a tighter coupling between inputs and weights. Rather than assigning an independent weight to every `(irrep_in1, irrep_in2, irrep_out)` path, it restricts weights to depend only on the `(irrep_in1, irrep_in2)` pair. This reduces parameter count and is the operation used in MACE and PaiNN architectures.

### Filter Irreps and Output Control

The constructor accepts an optional `filter_irreps_out` parameter that controls which irrep degrees appear in the output. When `None`, all valid output irreps from coupling `irreps_in1` with `irreps_in2` are included. When specified as a sequence of `Irrep` objects, only those degrees are retained [tp_channel_wise.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_channel_wise.py#L59-L63):

```python
# All valid output irreps from coupling
tp = cuet.ChannelWiseTensorProduct(
    irreps_in1="16x0e + 16x1o + 16x2e",
    irreps_in2="0e + 1o",
)

# Only specific output degrees
tp = cuet.ChannelWiseTensorProduct(
    irreps_in1="16x0e + 16x1o + 16x2e",
    irreps_in2="0e + 1o",
    filter_irreps_out=[cue.Irrep("O3", "0e"), cue.Irrep("O3", "1o")],
)
```

### Uniform Segment Constraint and Method Selection

A critical implementation detail is that the `"uniform_1d"` CUDA kernel requires all polynomial segments to have the same shape. The constructor checks this condition via `e2.all_same_segment_shape()` and falls back to `"naive"` with a warning if segments are non-uniform [tp_channel_wise.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_channel_wise.py#L115-L148). If you explicitly request `"uniform_1d"` with non-uniform segments, a `ValueError` is raised.

### Indexed Forward Pass

Unlike `FullyConnectedTensorProduct`, the channel-wise variant supports **index-based gathering and scattering** through optional `indices_1`, `indices_2`, and `indices_out` parameters [tp_channel_wise.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_channel_wise.py#L231-L256). These enable efficient message-passing patterns where only a subset of channels participate per edge or node, avoiding materializing full intermediate tensors.

Sources: [tp_channel_wise.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_channel_wise.py#L59-L148), [tp_channel_wise.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_channel_wise.py#L186-L258)

## Equivariant Linear Layer

The `Linear` operation is the equivariant generalization of a standard `nn.Linear`. It maps between two irreps spaces while preserving irrep degree — scalars map to scalars, vectors to vectors, and so on. Within each irrep degree, an independent linear transformation mixes the multiplicity channels.

### Weight Classes

A distinctive feature of `Linear` is the `weight_classes` parameter, which enables **multiple distinct weight matrices** that can be selected per batch element via `weight_indices` at forward time [linear.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/linear.py#L64). This is useful in architectures like MACE where different chemical elements use different linear projections:

```python
linear = cuet.Linear(
    irreps_in="16x0e + 16x1o",
    irreps_out="16x0e + 16x1o",
    weight_classes=5,  # e.g., 5 chemical elements
)
output = linear(x, weight_indices=element_ids)  # per-node element assignment
```

When `weight_classes > 1`, the internal weight parameter has shape `(weight_classes, weight_numel)` and `weight_indices` must be provided at forward time. This mechanism avoids materializing per-element copies of the full input tensor [linear.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/linear.py#L163-L183).

### Execution Methods

The `Linear` layer supports three execution methods — `"naive"` (default), `"fused_tp"`, and `"indexed_linear"` — as verified by the test suite [linear_test.py](cuequivariance_torch/tests/operations/linear_test.py#L279). The `"indexed_linear"` method is particularly relevant when `weight_classes > 1`, as it can use optimized indexed GEMM operations rather than gathering per-class weights into a dense matrix.

Sources: [linear.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/linear.py#L54-L192), [linear_test.py](cuequivariance_torch/tests/operations/linear_test.py#L276-L288)

## Shared Architectural Patterns

All three operations share a consistent internal architecture that is worth understanding as a unified pattern.

### Layout Transposition Pipeline

Every operation constructs `TransposeIrrepsLayout` modules for its inputs and outputs. These modules convert between the user-specified layout (e.g., `cue.mul_ir` for e3nn compatibility) and the internal layout required by the descriptor's `SegmentedPolynomial` [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L122-L141). This transposition happens on every forward call and is the mechanism that makes the operations agnostic to the irreps memory layout:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["User Tensor\n(layout_in)"] --> B["TransposeIrrepsLayout"]
    B --> C["Internal Layout\n(descriptor layout)"]
    C --> D["SegmentedPolynomial\n(computation)"]
    D --> E["Internal Layout\n(descriptor layout)"]
    E --> F["TransposeIrrepsLayout"]
    F --> G["Output Tensor\n(layout_out)"]
```

### Descriptor-Driven Instantiation

Each operation follows the same initialization sequence: (1) call a `descriptors.*` function to obtain a `Descriptor` object, (2) assert the expected subscript pattern, (3) extract `weight_numel` from the descriptor's polynomial operands, (4) construct layout transposers, and (5) instantiate `SegmentedPolynomial` with the chosen method. This pattern ensures that the mathematical definition lives in `cuequivariance.descriptors` (see [Tensor Product Descriptors](9-tensor-product-descriptors)) while the PyTorch operation layer handles device management, parameter storage, and layout conversion.

### Deprecated Fallback Parameter

All operations accept a deprecated `use_fallback` parameter that is being migrated to the explicit `method` parameter. The mapping is straightforward: `use_fallback=True` → `method="naive"`, `use_fallback=False` or `None` → the operation's default CUDA method (`"fused_tp"` or `"uniform_1d"`) [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L128-L141).

Sources: [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L100-L153), [tp_channel_wise.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_channel_wise.py#L122-L163), [linear.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/linear.py#L89-L134)

## FullyConnectedTensorProductConv: Message Passing Layer

While the three operations above are primitive building blocks, `FullyConnectedTensorProductConv` in `cuequivariance_torch/layers/` is a **composite layer** that combines a `FullyConnectedTensorProduct` with graph scatter operations and an optional MLP, implementing the full message-passing update used in architectures like DiffDock.

### Mathematical Formulation

The layer computes a per-node feature update by gathering messages from neighbor nodes, applying a tensor product with edge spherical harmonics, and reducing over the neighborhood [tp_conv_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/layers/tp_conv_fully_connected.py#L29-L97):

$$\mathbf{h}_a \leftarrow \text{BatchNorm}\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}_a|} \sum_{b \in \mathcal{N}_a} \left[\mathbf{h}_b \otimes_{\psi_{ab}} Y(\hat{r}_{ab})\right] \cdot c_{ab}\right)$$

where `ψ_ab` are path weights generated by an optional MLP from edge and node embeddings, and `c_ab` is an optional edge envelope attenuation factor.

### Internal Composition

The layer internally composes several components [tp_conv_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/layers/tp_conv_fully_connected.py#L139-L153):

- A `FullyConnectedTensorProduct` with `shared_weights=False` (per-edge weights)
- An optional `nn.Sequential` MLP that maps edge embeddings to tensor product weights
- An optional `BatchNorm` applied to the aggregated output
- Graph scatter/reduce utilities (`scatter_reduce`) for message aggregation

### Three MLP Usage Patterns

The constructor supports three patterns for weight generation, controlled by the `mlp_channels` parameter:

1. **No MLP** (`mlp_channels=None`): Edge embeddings are used directly as tensor product weights. Their last dimension must exactly equal `tp.weight_numel`.
2. **Single embedding input**: The MLP transforms the full edge embedding into weights. The MLP's last layer outputs `weight_numel` features.
3. **Split scalar inputs**: When `src_scalars` and `dst_scalars` are provided at forward time, the first MLP layer's weight matrix is split into three sections (edge, source, destination). Each section performs a separate linear projection before indexing, enabling more efficient computation by avoiding concatenation of large node feature tensors [tp_conv_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/layers/tp_conv_fully_connected.py#L221-L245).

```python
# Pattern 1: No MLP — direct weight mapping
conv = cuet.FullyConnectedTensorProductConv(
    in_irreps, sh_irreps, out_irreps,
    mlp_channels=None,
)
output = conv(node_features, edge_sh, edge_weights, graph)

# Pattern 2: MLP with hidden layers
conv = cuet.FullyConnectedTensorProductConv(
    in_irreps, sh_irreps, out_irreps,
    mlp_channels=[6, 16, 16],
    mlp_activation=nn.ReLU(),
)
output = conv(node_features, edge_sh, edge_emb, graph)

# Pattern 3: Split scalar inputs for efficient GEMM
output = conv(node_features, edge_sh, edge_emb, graph,
              src_scalars=node_scalar_feats, dst_scalars=node_scalar_feats)
```

Sources: [tp_conv_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/layers/tp_conv_fully_connected.py#L29-L167), [tp_conv_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/layers/tp_conv_fully_connected.py#L200-L265), [layers/__init__.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/layers/__init__.py#L15-L21)

## Method Selection Guide

Choosing the right execution method involves understanding the trade-offs between CUDA kernel availability, segment uniformity, and numerical precision.

| Method | Operation | Requirement | Performance | Precision Control |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `"fused_tp"` | FCTP, Linear | CUDA available | Best (single kernel launch) | `math_dtype` |
| `"uniform_1d"` | CWTP | Uniform segment shapes | Good (specialized kernel) | `math_dtype` |
| `"naive"` | All | None (pure PyTorch) | Baseline | Follows input dtype |
| `"indexed_linear"` | Linear | `weight_classes > 1` | Optimized for indexing | `math_dtype` |

The `math_dtype` parameter controls the precision of internal computations. When set to `None`, the default behavior varies by method: `"fused_tp"` falls back to the weight `dtype` [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L143), while `"naive"` follows the input tensor dtype. Setting `math_dtype="float64"` forces double-precision accumulation, which can be important for numerical stability in higher-order irreps.

> [!TIP]
> For production deployments, prefer `method="fused_tp"` (FCTP/Linear) or `method="uniform_1d"` (CWTP) whenever possible. The `"naive"` method should only be used for debugging, CPU execution, or when the uniform segment constraint cannot be satisfied. The test suite exercises all method/layout/precision combinations to verify correctness [fully_connected_test.py](cuequivariance_torch/tests/operations/fully_connected_test.py#L43-L54).

Sources: [tp_fully_connected.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_fully_connected.py#L128-L153), [tp_channel_wise.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_channel_wise.py#L131-L163), [linear_test.py](cuequivariance_torch/tests/operations/linear_test.py#L276-L288)

## Export and TorchScript Compatibility

All three core operations support TorchScript export via `torch.jit.script`, `torch.jit.trace`, and `torch.compile`. The test suite verifies this across all layout/weight configurations through a parameterized `test_export` function [fully_connected_test.py](cuequivariance_torch/tests/operations/fully_connected_test.py#L99-L114), [channel_wise_test.py](cuequivariance_torch/tests/operations/channel_wise_test.py#L97-L114), [linear_test.py](cuequivariance_torch/tests/operations/linear_test.py#L205-L220). The `extra_repr` methods are decorated with `@torch.jit.ignore` to avoid scripting issues with string formatting [tp_channel_wise.py](cuequivariance_torch/cuequivariance_torch/operations/tp_channel_wise.py#L178).

## Continuing the Exploration

The tensor product operations documented here are the consumer-facing API that delegates to lower-level primitives. To understand how these operations achieve their performance characteristics, see [CUDA Primitive Implementations](13-cuda-primitive-implementations) for the kernel-level details. For the mathematical foundations that define which irrep couplings are valid and how descriptors encode them, refer to [Tensor Product Descriptors](9-tensor-product-descriptors). To see how these operations compose into complete equivariant architectures, continue to [Symmetric Contraction Layer](14-symmetric-contraction-layer) and [Model Examples: MACE and NequIP](21-model-examples-mace-and-nequip).

# JAX Equivariant Polynomial



The `cuex.equivariant_polynomial` function is the primary entry point for computing **group-equivariant polynomial transformations** in cuEquivariance's JAX backend. It wraps the lower-level `segmented_polynomial` primitive with representation-aware input validation, automatic output shape inference, and seamless `RepArray` handling — letting you focus on the mathematical structure of your equivariant layers rather than the mechanics of buffer management.

## Architecture: Where It Sits

The equivariant polynomial system in JAX spans two packages and three conceptual layers. Understanding this stack is essential because each layer has a distinct role: **descriptors** define *what* to compute, the **primitive** defines *how* JAX compiles it, and `equivariant_polynomial()` bridges the two with **type safety**.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Descriptor["cuequivariance (CPU)"]
        EP["EquivariantPolynomial<br/>inputs/outputs: tuple of Rep<br/>polynomial: SegmentedPolynomial"]
        SP["SegmentedPolynomial<br/>inputs/outputs: SegmentedOperand<br/>operations: list of Operation × STP"]
        STP["SegmentedTensorProduct<br/>paths, subscripts, segments"]
        EP --> SP --> STP
    end

    subgraph JAXBackend["cuequivariance_jax (GPU/CPU)"]
        EPF["equivariant_polynomial()<br/>RepArray validation & wrapping"]
        SPJ["segmented_polynomial()<br/>JAX primitive dispatch"]
        PRIM["segmented_polynomial_p<br/>custom JAX primitive"]
        EPF --> SPJ --> PRIM
    end

    subgraph Transforms["JAX Transformations"]
        JIT["jit"]
        GRAD["grad"]
        VMAP["vmap"]
        JVP["jvp"]
    end

    EPF -.->|"wraps .polynomial"| SP
    PRIM -->|"delegates to"| SP
    JIT --> PRIM
    GRAD --> PRIM
    VMAP --> PRIM
    JVP --> PRIM
```

The `EquivariantPolynomial` descriptor lives in the core `cuequivariance` package and carries group representation metadata (`inputs` and `outputs` as `cue.Rep` objects) alongside a `SegmentedPolynomial` that encodes the actual computation graph [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance/cuequivariance/group_theory/equivariant_polynomial.py#L28-L75). The JAX wrapper function extracts `.polynomial` for computation while using the representation metadata for input validation and output labeling.

## Function Signature and Parameters

The `equivariant_polynomial` function accepts an `EquivariantPolynomial` descriptor and a list of `RepArray` (or plain `jax.Array` for scalar inputs), then returns typed `RepArray` outputs.

Sources: [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L25-L38)

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `poly` | `cue.EquivariantPolynomial` | Yes | The equivariant polynomial descriptor defining the computation and representation constraints |
| `inputs` | `list[RepArray \| jax.Array]` | Yes | Input tensors; each must be a `RepArray` with matching representation, or a plain `jax.Array` for scalar representations |
| `outputs_shape_dtype` | `list[ShapeDtypeStruct] \| ShapeDtypeStruct \| None` | No | Shape/dtype for outputs. When `None`, shapes are inferred from inputs. Last dimension accepts `-1` for auto-inference from the descriptor |
| `indices` | `list[None \| jax.Array \| tuple] \| None` | No | Per-operand index arrays for scatter/gather. Length must equal `poly.num_operands`. Use `None` for unindexed operands |
| `method` | `str` | Yes* | Computation backend: `"naive"`, `"uniform_1d"`, or `"indexed_linear"` |
| `math_dtype` | `str \| None` | No | Overrides computation dtype. See [`segmented_polynomial`](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L84-L96) for supported values per method |
| `options` | `dict \| None` | No | Method-specific options, including `"math_dtype"` and other configuration keys |
| `name` | `str \| None` | No | Operation name for profiling and debugging. Defaults to `"equivariant_polynomial"` |

*The `method` parameter became required starting in v0.6.0. Passing `""` raises a descriptive error guiding migration [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L165-L170).

## Input Validation Pipeline

Before any computation begins, `equivariant_polynomial` performs a rigorous validation pass. This is a key differentiator from calling `segmented_polynomial` directly — the representation-aware wrapper catches type mismatches early.

The validation proceeds through three stages. First, input count is checked against `poly.num_inputs` [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L114-L117). Second, each input is verified: `RepArray` inputs must have `rep(-1) == poly.inputs[i]`, while plain `jax.Array` inputs are only permitted for scalar representations (and must have `x.shape[-1] == rep.dim`) [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L119-L134). Third, indices length must equal `poly.num_operands` [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L141-L144).

After validation, `RepArray` inputs are unwrapped to their underlying `jax.Array` via `getattr(x, "array", x)` [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L136), and the raw arrays are dispatched to `segmented_polynomial`. The raw output arrays are then re-wrapped as `RepArray` objects using the descriptor's output representations [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L198).

## Automatic Output Shape Inference

When `outputs_shape_dtype` is `None`, the function automatically infers output shapes by broadcasting the batch dimensions of all inputs, accounting for index configurations. This inference handles both unindexed and indexed operands, and even `Repeats` objects for repeated-index patterns [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L148-L176).

The inference logic broadcasts shapes across all indexed and unindexed inputs using `jnp.broadcast_shapes`, then appends the representation dimension from `rep.dim` for each output. The dtype is inferred via `jnp.result_type(*inputs)`. A single-output polynomial automatically unwraps from list to scalar return; multi-output polynomials always return a list.

Two constraints apply to inference: output indices cannot be provided without explicit `outputs_shape_dtype`, and zero-input polynomials require explicit shape specification [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L148-L156).

> [!TIP]
> When providing output indices for scatter patterns (e.g., message-passing on graphs), you **must** specify `outputs_shape_dtype` explicitly. The function cannot infer output sizes when indices determine the scatter target, because the broadcast shape depends on index structure rather than input shapes alone.

## Computation Methods

The underlying `segmented_polynomial` dispatches to one of three implementation strategies. Method selection is driven by the polynomial structure and hardware availability.

Sources: [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L518-L549)

| Method | Backend | Use Case | Index Support |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"naive"` | JAX (any platform) | Reference implementation, always works, used for correctness validation | Full (including slice indices) |
| `"uniform_1d"` | CUDA | High-performance path for polynomials with a single uniform mode | Partial (integer index arrays) |
| `"indexed_linear"` | CUDA | Optimized for linear layers with partitioned/repeated weights | Partial (Repeats mode) |

When `"uniform_1d"` or `"indexed_linear"` is requested on a non-CUDA platform, the system falls back to `"naive"` with a warning [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L519-L525). The `Repeats` indexing mode is only supported by `"naive"` and `"indexed_linear"` [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L537-L541).

## JAX Transformation Support

The computation is implemented as a custom JAX primitive (`segmented_polynomial_p`) with full transformation rule coverage. This is what enables `jit`, `grad`, and `vmap` to work transparently through `equivariant_polynomial`.

Sources: [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L780-L801)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Rules["Transformation Rules"]
        ABSTRACT["abstract_eval<br/>shape/dtype inference"]
        JVP["jvp_rule<br/>forward-mode AD"]
        TRANSPOSE["transpose_rule<br/>reverse-mode AD"]
        BATCH["batching_rule<br/>vmap support"]
        DCE["dce_rule<br/>dead code elimination"]
    end

    PRIM["segmented_polynomial_p"] --> ABSTRACT
    PRIM --> JVP
    PRIM --> TRANSPOSE
    PRIM --> BATCH
    PRIM --> DCE

    CUDA["CUDA lowering"] --> PRIM
    CPU["CPU lowering"] --> PRIM
```

Each rule is registered at the primitive level [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L780-L801):

- **Abstract eval** (`segmented_polynomial_abstract_eval`): Provides shape and dtype information during JAX tracing [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L467-L476)
- **JVP** (`segmented_polynomial_jvp`): Forward-mode automatic differentiation, computing tangent outputs from primal and tangent inputs [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L552-L612)
- **Transpose** (`segmented_polynomial_transpose`): Reverse-mode AD for gradient computation via `jax.grad` [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L613-L675)
- **Batching** (`segmented_polynomial_batching`): Maps a batch dimension across inputs/outputs for `jax.vmap` [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L676-L729)
- **DCE** (`segmented_polynomial_dce`): Dead code elimination removes unused operands during partial evaluation [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L731-L778)

The DCE rule is particularly noteworthy — it filters out unused inputs and outputs at the JAXpr level, preventing unnecessary computation during partial evaluation (e.g., when `grad` only needs gradients for some inputs).

## Practical Usage Examples

### Basic Spherical Harmonics

The simplest usage pattern creates a descriptor, prepares a `RepArray` input, and calls the function. The spherical harmonics descriptor computes rotation-equivariant features from a 3D vector.

Sources: [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L67-L83)

```python
import cuequivariance as cue
import cuequivariance_jax as cuex
import jax.numpy as jnp

# Create descriptor for SO(3) spherical harmonics up to degree 2
e = cue.descriptors.spherical_harmonics(cue.SO3(1), [0, 1, 2])

# Prepare input: a unit vector along y-axis as an l=1 (vector) RepArray
with cue.assume(cue.SO3, cue.ir_mul):
    x = cuex.RepArray("1", jnp.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]))

# Compute — returns a RepArray with irreps 0+1+2
result = cuex.equivariant_polynomial(e, [x], method="naive")
```

### Indexed Computation for Message Passing

In graph neural networks, node features are indexed by edge lists. The `indices` parameter enables this pattern directly, scattering results into per-node output buffers.

Sources: [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L86-L104), [equivariant_polynomial_test.py](cuequivariance_jax/tests/equivariant_polynomial_test.py#L60-L118)

```python
from cuequivariance_jax import segmented_polynomials as sp

# Describe a symmetric contraction for a MACE-like architecture
e = cue.descriptors.symmetric_contraction(
    64 * cue.Irreps("SO3", "0 + 1 + 2"),
    64 * cue.Irreps("SO3", "0 + 1"),
    [0, 1, 2, 3]
)

num_nodes, num_edges = 30, 100
inputs = [
    cuex.randn(jax.random.key(0), rep, (Z,), jnp.float64)
    for Z, rep in zip([num_edges] * e.num_inputs, e.inputs)
]
# Override first input batch to num_nodes (node features)
inputs[0] = cuex.randn(jax.random.key(0), e.inputs[0], (num_nodes,), jnp.float64)

# Edge index arrays for scatter/gather
indices = [None] * e.num_operands
indices[0] = jax.random.randint(jax.random.key(1), (num_edges,), 0, num_nodes, jnp.int32)
indices[-1] = jax.random.randint(jax.random.key(1), (num_edges,), 0, num_nodes, jnp.int32)

output_spec = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((num_nodes, e.outputs[0].dim), jnp.float64)
result = cuex.equivariant_polynomial(e, inputs, output_spec, indices, method="uniform_1d")
```

### Differentiation

The custom primitive rules enable full `jax.grad` support, including higher-order derivatives as validated by the test suite [equivariant_polynomial_test.py](cuequivariance_jax/tests/equivariant_polynomial_test.py#L24-L38).

```python
def loss(w, x):
    return cuex.equivariant_polynomial(e, [w, x], method="naive").array.sum() ** 2

# Single backward
grad_fn = jax.grad(loss, argnums=0)
grads = grad_fn(w, x)

# Double backward is also supported
grad_of_grad = jax.grad(lambda w, x: jax.grad(loss, 1)(w, x).array.sum() ** 2, argnums=0)
```

## Relationship to Segmented Polynomial

The `equivariant_polynomial` function is intentionally thin. Its entire computational body delegates to `segmented_polynomial`, extracting `poly.polynomial` (the underlying `SegmentedPolynomial`) and passing the unwrapped array data [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L187-L197). The value it adds is:

1. **Type safety**: Verifies that `RepArray` inputs carry the correct group representations
2. **Convenience**: Automatically infers output shapes and wraps results back into `RepArray`
3. **Single/multi output normalization**: Returns a scalar `RepArray` for single-output polynomials and a list for multi-output, matching the descriptor structure

For scenarios requiring direct control over raw `jax.Array` buffers — such as custom JAXpr transformations or integration with non-representation-aware code — calling `segmented_polynomial` directly is the appropriate path. See [JAX Segmented Polynomial Variants](17-jax-segmented-polynomial-variants) for the full details on that layer.

> [!TIP]
> The `precision` parameter is deprecated in favor of `math_dtype`. Passing any value other than `"undefined"` (the default) raises a `ValueError` directing you to use `math_dtype` or `options` instead [equivariant_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/equivariant_polynomial.py#L109-L112).

## Performance Considerations

The `uniform_1d` CUDA method provides significant speedup over `naive` for suitable polynomial structures (those with a single uniform mode). The test suite validates numerical equivalence between `"naive"` and `"uniform_1d"` at `float64` precision with tight tolerances (`atol=1e-12`), confirming both forward and backward passes produce identical results [equivariant_polynomial_test.py](cuequivariance_jax/tests/equivariant_polynomial_test.py#L92-L118).

For multi-device scenarios, the underlying CUDA kernel requires manual sharding via `jax.shard_map` to achieve proper performance — automatic sharding is not supported for this custom primitive [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L157-L162).

## Next Steps

- **[JAX Segmented Polynomial Variants](17-jax-segmented-polynomial-variants)** — Deep dive into the three implementation methods (`naive`, `uniform_1d`, `indexed_linear`) and their index configuration system
- **[RepArray System](19-reparray-system)** — Understanding the representation-aware array type that flows through `equivariant_polynomial`
- **[Equivariant Polynomial Hierarchy](8-equivariant-polynomial-hierarchy)** — How `EquivariantPolynomial` relates to `SegmentedPolynomial` and `SegmentedTensorProduct` in the descriptor system
- **[Automatic Differentiation Support](20-automatic-differentiation-support)** — Detailed analysis of JVP, transpose, and batching rules
- **[Model Examples: MACE and NequIP](21-model-examples-mace-and-nequip)** — End-to-end model implementations using `equivariant_polynomial`

# JAX Segmented Polynomial Variants



The JAX backend exposes a single entry point — `segmented_polynomial()` — that dispatches to one of three carefully stratified execution backends. Each variant occupies a distinct niche in the performance–flexibility spectrum, from pure-JAX portability to GPU-native fused kernels. This page documents their internal architectures, dispatch logic, and the JAX transformation machinery that unifies them behind a shared primitive.

## Variant Landscape and Dispatch Architecture

All three variants converge on a single `segmented_polynomial` function in [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L51-L62). The `method` parameter — now mandatory since v0.6.0 — selects the execution strategy at call time. The dispatch decision is enforced inside the implementation handler at [segmented_polynomial_impl](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L482-L549), which also applies a platform guard: if a CUDA-only method is requested on a non-CUDA backend, it silently falls back to `"naive"` with a warning.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["segmented_polynomial()"] -->|"method='naive'"| N["execute_naive()"]
    A -->|"method='uniform_1d'"| U["execute_uniform_1d()"]
    A -->|"method='indexed_linear'"| I["execute_indexed_linear()"]

    N -->|"REPEATED mode detected"| I2["execute_indexed_linear(run_kernel=False)"]
    N -->|"no REPEATED"| N2["Pure JAX einsum strategies"]

    U -->|"CUDA kernel"| CUDA["cuequivariance_ops_jax.uniform_1d"]

    I -->|"pattern match"| I3["cuequivariance_ops_jax.indexed_linear"]
    I -->|"no match"| I4["Pure JAX fallback einsum"]
```

The following table summarises the core trade-offs at a glance:

| Variant | Backend | Indexing Modes Supported | Typical Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"naive"` | Pure JAX (all platforms) | All three modes | Testing, prototyping, non-CUDA environments |
| `"uniform_1d"` | CUDA via `cuequivariance_ops_jax` | `BATCHED_OR_SHARED`, `INDEXED` only | Single-mode tensor products with uniform segment shapes |
| `"indexed_linear"` | CUDA + JAX fallback | All three modes | Linear layers with partitioned/repeated weights |

Sources: [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L51-L62), [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L530-L549)

## The Indexing Mode System

Before examining each variant, it is essential to understand the indexing infrastructure defined in [indexing_mode.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/indexing_mode.py#L18-L26). Each buffer (input or output) can carry an optional multi-axis index, and each axis of that index is classified by one of three `IndexingMode` values. This classification drives both correctness semantics and kernel selection.

| Mode | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `BATCHED_OR_SHARED` | No explicit index; the dimension participates in broadcasting or is shared across buffers | Standard batched tensor product |
| `INDEXED` | A JAX integer array that selects along this dimension | Per-atom indexing in molecular graphs |
| `REPEATED` | A `Repeats` object specifying variable replication counts per element | Partitioned weight matrices where each partition has a different count |

The `Repeats` dataclass in [utils.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/utils.py#L76-L98) wraps a repeat-count array and is registered as a JAX pytree node, making it transparent to JAX's tree utilities. During index sanitisation in the main function (lines 271–298), `Repeats` objects are unwrapped to their underlying arrays while retaining the `REPEATED` mode classification in the parallel `index_mode` structure.

Sources: [indexing_mode.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/indexing_mode.py#L18-L26), [utils.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/utils.py#L76-L98), [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L271-L298)

## Naive Variant: Pure JAX Execution

The `execute_naive` function in [segmented_polynomial_naive.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_naive.py#L39-L127) is the universal fallback. It operates entirely through JAX primitives — primarily `jnp.einsum`, `jnp.take`, `jnp.stack`, and `jnp.sum` — making it compatible with any platform JAX targets (CPU, GPU, TPU). The implementation iterates over each `operation` in the polynomial, scatters indexed inputs into a common batch coordinate space via `scatter()`, computes the segmented tensor product via `tp_list_list()`, concatenates the result segments back to full operand size via `sum_cat_list_list()`, and then gathers the output back into the original index space via `gather()`.

### Einsum Strategies

The `tp_list_list` function at [line 172](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_naive.py#L172-L415) is the computational core. It dynamically selects one of six algorithms based on segment shape uniformity and path count:

| Algorithm | Condition | Strategy |
|---|---|---|
| `"sliced"` | Non-uniform segment shapes | Direct slicing per path — no reshaping required |
| `"stacked"` | Uniform shapes, path count ≤ threshold | Reshape operands to `(batch, num_segments, segment_dim)`, `jnp.take` per path |
| `"compact_stacked"` | Uniform shapes, path count > threshold | Vectorise accumulated einsum over path groups to reduce launch overhead |
| `"indexed_vmap"` | Non-uniform shapes, many paths | `jax.vmap` over paths with `at[].add()` scatter |
| `"indexed_compact"` | Non-uniform shapes, many paths | Fully vectorised einsum with `at[].add()` scatter |
| `"indexed_for_loop"` | Non-uniform shapes, fallback | `jax.lax.fori_loop` — least XLA-friendly, last resort |

The threshold for switching from `"stacked"`/`"sliced"` to compact strategies is controlled by the `CUEQUIVARIANCE_MAX_PATH_UNROLL` environment variable, defaulting to 1000 paths.

### REPEATED Mode Delegation

When any buffer carries `IndexingMode.REPEATED`, `execute_naive` immediately delegates to `execute_indexed_linear` with `run_kernel=False` ([line 83](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_naive.py#L83-L87)). This fallback uses the indexed_linear variant's pure-JAX einsum path rather than its CUDA kernel, keeping the naive variant fully platform-portable while reusing the REPEATED handling logic.

### Math Dtype Configuration

The `math_dtype_for_naive` helper in [utils.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/utils.py#L102-L119) maps the `math_dtype` option to a JAX compute dtype and `jax.lax.Precision` enum. Setting `math_dtype="tensor_float32"` yields `jnp.float32` with `Precision.HIGH` (TF32 mode on Ampere+ GPUs). Any standard JAX dtype name (e.g., `"float16"`, `"bfloat16"`) is resolved to its JAX counterpart with `Precision.HIGHEST`.

Sources: [segmented_polynomial_naive.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_naive.py#L39-L127), [segmented_polynomial_naive.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_naive.py#L172-L415), [utils.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/utils.py#L102-L119)

## Uniform 1D Variant: CUDA Fused Kernel

The `execute_uniform_1d` function in [segmented_polynomial_uniform_1d.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_uniform_1d.py#L35-L198) targets maximum throughput for a specific but common case: polynomials composed of segmented tensor products that share exactly one uniform mode across all operands. This variant delegates entirely to `cuequivariance_ops_jax.uniform_1d`, a precompiled CUDA kernel.

### Precondition Pipeline

Before invoking the kernel, the function applies a rigorous validation and transformation pipeline:

1. **Coefficient flattening** ([line 80](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_uniform_1d.py#L80-L87)): All coefficient modes are flattened — `coefficient_subscripts` must become empty. This fails fast with a descriptive error if coefficient modes exist.

2. **Mode squeezing and canonicalisation** ([line 88](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_uniform_1d.py#L88-L89)): Singleton modes are removed and subscripts are canonicalised.

3. **Single-mode enforcement** ([line 91](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_uniform_1d.py#L91-L93)): If an STP has zero modes, a dummy mode `u` with extent 1 is appended.

4. **Uniform segment shape validation** ([line 107](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_uniform_1d.py#L107-L121)): Every operand in every STP must have uniform segment shapes within that STP. When this fails, the error message computes the GCD of mode extents and suggests applying `split_mode()` as a resolution.

5. **Single uniform extent** ([line 141](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_uniform_1d.py#L141-L145)): All STPs must share the same mode extent (e.g., `u=3` everywhere).

6. **Buffer reshaping** ([line 121](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_uniform_1d.py#L121-L127)): Buffers are reshaped from `(*batch, operand_size)` to `(*batch, num_segments, segment_size)` based on STP operand metadata.

### Kernel Invocation

After validation, the polynomial's operations and paths are converted to plain data objects (`Operation`, `Path` from `cuequivariance_ops_jax`) and passed to the `uniform_1d` CUDA function ([line 172](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_uniform_1d.py#L172-L189)). The `math_dtype` option is limited to standard floating-point types: `float32`, `float64`, `float16`, `bfloat16`. The name is sanitised to alphanumeric characters for use as a CUDA kernel identifier.

> [!TIP]
> The `uniform_1d` method requires the `cuequivariance_ops_jax` package (version ≥ 0.4.0.dev). If your polynomial has multiple modes or non-uniform segment shapes, apply `polynomial.flatten_modes()` or `polynomial.split_mode()` before calling this variant to meet its preconditions.

Sources: [segmented_polynomial_uniform_1d.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_uniform_1d.py#L35-L198)

## Indexed Linear Variant: Hybrid CUDA + JAX

The `execute_indexed_linear` function in [segmented_polynomial_indexed_linear.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_indexed_linear.py#L42-L127) is the most architecturally interesting variant. It is designed for equivariant linear layers where weight matrices are partitioned by irrep type with variable partition sizes — the pattern used in MACE and NequIP-style models.

### Execution Flow

The outer loop in [execute_indexed_linear](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_indexed_linear.py#L42-L127) iterates over the polynomial's operations. For each operation, it calls `tp_list_list` ([line 138](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_indexed_linear.py#L138-L196)), which slices input and output `Buffer` objects per path and invokes the central `ein` function. Unlike the naive variant, results are accumulated via `io_buffers[b_out] += out` rather than scatter/gather, because the indexed linear pattern always operates in a shared batch space.

### Pattern-Matched CUDA Kernel Dispatch

The `ein` function at [line 198](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_indexed_linear.py#L198-L427) is where the critical dispatch occurs. It constructs an Einstein summation formula from the subscripts and batch dimensions, then checks whether the formula **and** the indexing mode combination match one of several hardcoded patterns. Each pattern corresponds to a specific linear algebra primitive:

| Formula Pattern | Mode Signature | Operation |
|---|---|---|
| `,Auv,Au->Av` | `(REPEATED, BATCHED, BATCHED)` | Partitioned weight right-multiply |
| `,Auv,Av->Au` | `(REPEATED, BATCHED, BATCHED)` | Partitioned weight left-multiply |
| `,Auv,Awu->Awv` | `(REPEATED, BATCHED, BATCHED)` | Partitioned right-multiply with extra mode |
| `,Au,Auv->Av` | `(BATCHED, REPEATED, BATCHED)` | Input left, weight repeated |
| `,Auv,Awv->Auw` | `(BATCHED, REPEATED, BATCHED)` | Input with extra mode, weight repeated |
| `,Au,Av->Auv` | `(BATCHED, BATCHED, REPEATED)` | Outer product into partitioned output |
| `,Auv,Auw->Awv` | `(BATCHED, BATCHED, REPEATED)` | Outer product with extra modes |

When a pattern matches and `run_kernel=True`, the function calls `cuequivariance_ops_jax.indexed_linear` with the appropriate layout strings. When no pattern matches, it falls through to a pure-JAX `jnp.einsum` call, preserving correctness across all input configurations.

### The `run_kernel` Parameter

The `run_kernel` flag controls whether CUDA kernel dispatch is attempted. The naive variant calls `execute_indexed_linear` with `run_kernel=False` to reuse the REPEATED-mode logic on non-CUDA platforms, while the direct `method="indexed_linear"` path sets it to `True` by default.

Sources: [segmented_polynomial_indexed_linear.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_indexed_linear.py#L42-L127), [segmented_polynomial_indexed_linear.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial_indexed_linear.py#L198-L427)

## JAX Primitive and Transformation Rules

All three variants are unified behind a single custom JAX primitive, `segmented_polynomial_p`, defined at [line 334](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L334-L335). This primitive is registered with the full suite of JAX transformation interpreters, enabling transparent use inside `jit`, `grad`, and `vmap` contexts.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "JAX Interpreter Registrations"
        ABS["abstract_eval<br/>shape inference"]
        CUDA["mlir.lowering (CUDA)"]
        CPU["mlir.lowering (fallback)"]
        JVP["JVP rule<br/>forward-mode AD"]
        TRANS["Transpose rule<br/>reverse-mode AD"]
        BATCH["Batching rule<br/>vmap support"]
        DCE["DCE rule<br/>dead code elimination"]
    end

    P["segmented_polynomial_p"] --> ABS
    P --> CUDA
    P --> CPU
    P --> JVP
    P --> TRANS
    P --> BATCH
    P --> DCE
```

### Forward-Mode AD (JVP)

The [segmented_polynomial_jvp](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L552-L612) rule computes forward-mode derivatives by generating a JVP polynomial from the base polynomial using `polynomial.jvp()`, which selects which inputs have non-zero tangents. The tangent computation shares the primals as additional inputs and remaps the index configuration via `_remap_indices_and_config` to account for the enlarged input set. Both primal and tangent outputs are computed via `segmented_polynomial_prim`, and zeros are passed through for inputs with `ad.Zero` tangents.

### Reverse-Mode AD (Transpose)

The [segmented_polynomial_transpose](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L613-L673) rule implements the VJP by constructing a transposed polynomial via `polynomial.transpose()`. Cotangents replace outputs as inputs, and undefined primal inputs become the new outputs. The transposed polynomial is then executed through the same `segmented_polynomial_prim` pathway, inheriting whatever method was specified for the forward pass.

### Batching (vmap)

The [segmented_polynomial_batching](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L676-L728) rule handles `jax.vmap` by inserting a new batch axis at dimension 0 for all inputs (using `jnp.expand_dims` for unbatched operands or `jnp.moveaxis` for already-batched ones). The new batch axis is marked as `BATCHED_OR_SHARED` in the index configuration, meaning it is never indexed — it simply broadcasts through the computation. The output batch axis is reported at position 0.

### Dead Code Elimination

The [segmented_polynomial_dce](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L731-L777) rule is the most sophisticated transformation handler. It operates at the JAXpr equation level, responding to JAX's partial evaluation pass. When some outputs are unused, the DCE rule:

1. Calls `polynomial.compute_only(used_outputs)` to prune unnecessary paths and operations.
2. Determines which inputs are still required via `polynomial.used_inputs()`.
3. Remaps the index configuration to eliminate unused index buffers.
4. Returns the modified equation with filtered inputs, outputs, and polynomial.

If **all** outputs are unused, the entire operation is eliminated, returning `None` for the equation and marking all inputs as unused.

> [!TIP]
> The DCE rule is what makes `jax.grad` efficient: when computing gradients with respect to only a subset of inputs, the transpose rule produces cotangents only for those inputs, and the DCE rule then eliminates all computation paths that don't contribute to those specific gradients. This can dramatically reduce the polynomial's operation count in the backward pass.

Sources: [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L334-L335), [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L552-L612), [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L613-L673), [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L676-L728), [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L731-L777), [segmented_polynomial.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/segmented_polynomials/segmented_polynomial.py#L780-L801)

## Practical Usage Patterns

### Selecting the Right Variant

The variant choice is driven by the polynomial's structure and the deployment environment. The following decision flow covers common scenarios:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["Is CUDA available?"]
    START -->|No| NAIVE["method='naive'"]
    START -->|Yes| CHECK1{"Does the polynomial<br/>have REPEATED indices?"}
    CHECK1 -->|Yes| CHECK2{"Is this a linear layer<br/>(partitioned weights)?"}
    CHECK1 -->|No| CHECK3{"Single uniform mode<br/>across all STPs?"}
    CHECK2 -->|Yes| INDEXED["method='indexed_linear'"]
    CHECK2 -->|No| NAIVE2["method='naive'<br/>(REPEATED not supported<br/>by uniform_1d)"]
    CHECK3 -->|Yes| UNIFORM["method='uniform_1d'"]
    CHECK3 -->|No| NAIVE3["method='naive'<br/>or reshape polynomial"]
```

### Math Dtype Options by Variant

| Option Key | `"naive"` | `"uniform_1d"` | `"indexed_linear"` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"float32"` / `"float64"` / `"float16"` / `"bfloat16"` | ✓ | ✓ | — |
| `"tensor_float32"` | ✓ (TF32 mode) | — | — |
| `"CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F"` / `"CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_FAST_TF32"` / `"CUBLAS_COMPUTE_64F"` etc. | — | — | ✓ |

When `math_dtype` is not specified, the compute dtype is automatically inferred from the input and output buffer dtypes.

### Multi-Device Sharding

The segmented polynomial primitive uses custom CUDA kernels that are not automatically sharded by JAX's implicit sharding. For multi-device execution, explicit sharding via `jax.shard_map` is required. Without it, computation will be redundantly replicated across devices, degrading rather than improving performance.


# Triangle Kernels



The `cuequivariance_jax.triangle` module provides a family of high-performance, fully differentiable triangle-structured neural network primitives targeting equivariant molecular modeling architectures such as AlphaFold2. These kernels encapsulate triangular attention and triangular multiplicative update operations — both operating on pairwise representations of shape `(N, N, D)` — with custom CUDA/Triton backends, custom JAX VJP rules, and `vmap`-compatible batching semantics. The module bridges the gap between research-grade equivariant models and production-grade GPU throughput.

## Module Architecture

The triangle subsystem is composed of four layers: the user-facing API (`triangle_multiplicative_update`, `triangle_attention`), two shared infrastructure primitives (`layer_norm_transpose`, `sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm`), and a cross-cutting utility layer handling precision enums, naive batching rules, and Triton-JAX interop. The public surface is intentionally narrow — only two functions and the `Precision` enum are exported from `__init__.py` [^1].

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Public API"
        TMU["triangle_multiplicative_update"]
        TA["triangle_attention"]
    end

    subgraph "Infrastructure Primitives"
        LNT["layer_norm_transpose"]
        SGD["sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm<br/>sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm_dual_x"]
    end

    subgraph "Shared Utilities"
        U["Precision enum"]
        NB["naive_batching_rule"]
        TU["triton_utils<br/>(triton_call, lowering)"]
    end

    TMU --> LNT
    TMU --> SGD
    TA --> NB
    SGD --> NB
    LNT --> NB
    LNT --> TU
    SGD --> TU

    style TMU fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style TA fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style LNT fill:#f5a623,color:#fff
    style SGD fill:#f5a623,color:#fff
    style U fill:#7ed321,color:#fff
    style NB fill:#7ed321,color:#fff
    style TU fill:#7ed321,color:#fff
```

Sources: [__init__.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/__init__.py#L21-L25)

## Precision Modes

All triangle kernels accept a `Precision` enum that controls the arithmetic precision of internal matrix multiplications. This enum maps directly to JAX dot-algorithm presets, providing fine-grained control over throughput versus numerical accuracy tradeoffs [^2].

| Enum Value | JAX Equivalent | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `Precision.DEFAULT` | `jax.lax.Precision.DEFAULT` | JAX default (typically TF32 on Ampere+) |
| `Precision.TF32` | `DotAlgorithmPreset.TF32_TF32_F32` | Explicit TF32 matmul, FP32 accumulation |
| `Precision.TF32x3` | `DotAlgorithmPreset.TF32_TF32_F32_X3` | TF32 with 3× accumulation channels |
| `Precision.IEEE` | `DotAlgorithmPreset.F32_F32_F32` | Full IEEE 754 FP32 throughout |

The `TF32x3` mode exploits tensor core instructions that accumulate three TF32 products per cycle, offering higher throughput at marginal precision cost — particularly relevant for the large-batch training regimes common in molecular dynamics.

Sources: [_utils.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_utils.py#L22-L37)

## Triangle Attention

`triangle_attention` implements scaled dot-product attention over pairwise representations with per-node masking. Unlike standard multi-head attention, this variant operates on tensors of shape `[B, N, H, S_qo, D]` where `N` indexes nodes (atoms/residues) and `S_qo`/`S_kv` index sequence positions within each node's neighborhood. The mask is per-node and broadcast across heads and query positions [^3].

### Mathematical Definition

The operation computes:

$$\text{Attention}_a(Q, K, V, M, T) = \sum_b \mathrm{softmax}_b\left(M_b \cdot (Q_a K_b^T + T_{ab}) + (1 - M_b) \cdot (-10^9)\right) V_b$$

where `Q`, `K`, `V` are query/key/value tensors, `M` is the boolean mask, and `T` is the additive bias (passed as `bias`). The softmax is stabilized via log-sum-exp with explicit max subtraction [^4].

### Tensor Shape Contract

| Parameter | Shape | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `q` | `[B, N, H, S_qo, D]` | Query tensor |
| `k` | `[B, N, H, S_kv, D]` | Key tensor |
| `v` | `[B, N, H, S_kv, D]` | Value tensor |
| `bias` | `[B, 1, H, S_qo, S_kv]` | Additive attention bias |
| `mask` | `[B, N, 1, 1, S_kv]` | Boolean mask (`True` = valid) |
| **output** | `[B, N, H, S_qo, D]` | Attention output |

The reference JAX implementation first scales queries, computes the `einsum` dot product, adds bias, applies the mask with a large negative fill value (`-1e9`), casts to float32 for the softmax (numerically stable via `logsumexp`), then casts back and projects through values [^4].

### Backend Dispatch and Custom Differentiation

The forward and backward passes are registered as separate JAX primitives (`triangle_attention_fwd` and `triangle_attention_bwd`) with platform-specific lowering. On CUDA, they delegate to `cuequivariance_ops_jax.triangle_attention_cuda_fwd/bwd` custom kernels; on CPU or when the ops package is unavailable, the pure-JAX reference path is used [^5].

A `custom_vjp` wrapper connects the two primitives for automatic differentiation, with `scale` and `precision` as non-differentiable arguments. The backward primitive takes the output gradient, attention output, log-sum-exp, and all original inputs to compute gradients for `q`, `k`, `v`, and `bias` [^6].

### Blackwell GPU Constraints

On Blackwell GPUs (compute capability 10.0/10.3), the specialized `sm100f` kernel imposes dimension constraints: hidden dimension ≤ 256 for forward and ≤ 128 for backward (bf16/fp16 only, divisible by 8), and `S_kv` must be a multiple of 8 for the forward kernel [^3].

> [!TIP]
> When using `triangle_attention` across multiple devices, manual sharding via `jax.shard_map` is required. Without explicit sharding, JAX's default replication strategy causes significant performance degradation due to cross-device communication overhead.

Sources: [_triangle_attention.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_triangle_attention.py#L35-L77), [_triangle_attention.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_triangle_attention.py#L84-L113), [_triangle_attention.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_triangle_attention.py#L161-L194), [_triangle_attention.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_triangle_attention.py#L248-L279)

## Triangle Multiplicative Update

`triangle_multiplicative_update` is the higher-level composite operation that implements the AlphaFold2-style triangular multiplicative module. It orchestrates four sub-steps: input layer normalization, sigmoid-gated dual linear projection, triangular contraction, output layer normalization, and output gating — all within a single differentiable function [^7].

### Computational Pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    X["x<br/>(..., N, N, D_in)"]
    LN1["layer_norm_transpose<br/>input normalization"]
    SG1["sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm<br/>input projection + gating"]
    SPLIT["split → a, b"]
    TRI["triangular contraction<br/>outgoing/incoming"]
    LN2["layer_norm_transpose<br/>output normalization"]
    SG2["sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm_dual_x<br/>output gating"]
    OUT["output<br/>(..., N, N, D_out)"]

    X --> LN1 --> SG1 --> SPLIT --> TRI --> LN2 --> SG2 --> OUT

    LN1 -.->|"x_in"| SG2
```

**Step 1 — Input normalization**: Layer normalization over the feature dimension using `layer_norm_transpose` with layout `"bijd->bijd"` (identity layout for 4D batch-sequence-sequence-feature tensors) [^7].

**Step 2 — Gated input projection**: A fused sigmoid-gated dual GEMM projects the normalized input through two weight matrices simultaneously — one for gating (`g_in_weight`) and one for the linear path (`p_in_weight`). The result `σ(x·g_in^T + b_g) · (x·p_in^T + b_p)` is transposed (via `transpose_out=True`) and split into tensors `a` and `b`, each of shape `[batch, 2·D_in, N, N]` reshaped to `[batch, D_in, N, N]` [^7].

**Step 3 — Triangular contraction**: Depending on the `direction` parameter, the contraction aggregates information along one axis of the pairwise matrix. For `"outgoing"`: `x[b,i,j] = Σ_k a[b,k,i] · b[b,k,j]`. For `"incoming"`: `x[b,i,j] = Σ_k a[b,i,k] · b[b,j,k]`. Both use `jnp.einsum` for the reduction [^7].

**Step 4 — Output normalization and gating**: The contracted result is normalized with a second `layer_norm_transpose` (layout `"dbij->bijd"`, transposing feature dimension to the last axis), then gated against the saved input-normalized activations `x_in` via `sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm_dual_x`, which takes two separate input tensors [^7].

### Parameter Contract

The function accepts 16 optional weight/bias parameters organized in four groups. When any weight is `None`, a JAX PRNG key must be provided for on-the-fly initialization:

| Group | Weight | Shape | Default Init |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input norm | `norm_in_weight` | `(D_in,)` | Ones |
| Input norm | `norm_in_bias` | `(D_in,)` | Zeros |
| Input projection | `p_in_weight` | `(2·D_in, D_in)` | LeCun normal |
| Input projection | `p_in_bias` | `(2·D_in,)` | None (no bias) |
| Input gating | `g_in_weight` | `(2·D_in, D_in)` | LeCun normal |
| Input gating | `g_in_bias` | `(2·D_in,)` | None (no bias) |
| Output norm | `norm_out_weight` | `(D_in,)` | Ones |
| Output norm | `norm_out_bias` | `(D_in,)` | Zeros |
| Output projection | `p_out_weight` | `(D_out, D_in)` | LeCun normal |
| Output projection | `p_out_bias` | `(D_out,)` | None (no bias) |
| Output gating | `g_out_weight` | `(D_out, D_in)` | LeCun normal |
| Output gating | `g_out_bias` | `(D_out,)` | None (no bias) |

The output dimension `D_out` defaults to `D_in` when neither `p_out_weight` nor `g_out_weight` is provided, but can differ if output weights with a different first dimension are supplied — enabling dimension-changing projections [^7].

### Fallback Threshold

The `fallback` parameter controls whether to use Triton-optimized or reference JAX implementations for the underlying `layer_norm_transpose` and `sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm` calls. When `fallback=None`, the system consults the environment variable `CUEQ_TRIMUL_FALLBACK_THRESHOLD` (default 100): if `seq_len ≤ threshold`, the reference path is used, otherwise the optimized path activates. This heuristic avoids Triton kernel launch overhead for small problem sizes [^8].

Sources: [_triangle_multiplicative_update.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_triangle_multiplicative_update.py#L109-L128), [_triangle_multiplicative_update.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_triangle_multiplicative_update.py#L310-L423), [_triangle_multiplicative_update.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_triangle_multiplicative_update.py#L31-L33)

## Infrastructure: Layer Norm Transpose

`layer_norm_transpose` is a layout-aware layer normalization primitive that supports flexible memory layout permutations between input and output tensors. It is exposed through the `layer_norm_transpose` function with a string-based layout specification (e.g., `"bijd->bijd"`, `"dbij->bijd"`) [^9].

### Layout System

The layout is specified as a string `"src->dst"` where each character represents a dimension. The `Layout` enum defines five concrete layout modes as integer codes used internally by the Triton kernels [^10].

| Layout String | Enum | Input Axes | Output Axes | Feature Dim Position |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `"nd->nd"` | `BND_BND` (0) | `(N, D)` | `(N, D)` | Last |
| `"bdn->bnd"` | `BDN_BND` (1) | `(B, D, N)` | `(B, N, D)` | Last |
| `"bnd->bdn"` | `BND_BDN` (2) | `(B, N, D)` | `(B, D, N)` | Middle |
| `"dbn->bnd"` | `DBN_BND` (3) | `(D, B, N)` | `(B, N, D)` | First → Last |
| `"bnd->dbn"` | `BND_DBN` (4) | `(B, N, D)` | `(D, B, N)` | Last → First |

The forward and backward passes are implemented as separate JAX primitives with custom abstract evaluation, Triton kernel lowering for GPU, and a pure JAX reference implementation for CPU. Custom VJP rules preserve the log-sum-exp and reciprocal-standard-deviation intermediates needed for numerically stable backpropagation [^9].

Sources: [_layer_norm_transpose.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_layer_norm_transpose.py#L36-L48), [_layer_norm_transpose.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_layer_norm_transpose.py#L497-L499)

## Infrastructure: Sigmoid-Gated Dual GEMM

The `sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm` family implements a fused operation that computes `σ(x·W_g^T + b_g) · (x·W_p^T + b_p)` — a sigmoid-gated linear projection — in a single kernel launch. Two variants exist: `sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm` (single input `x`) and `sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm_dual_x` (separate inputs `x1`, `x2`) [^11].

### Core Operation

For `sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm`, given input `x` of shape `(*, M, K)`:

1. Compute gate path: `g = x @ W_g^T + b_g` → shape `(*, M, N)`
2. Compute projection path: `p = x @ W_p^T + b_p` → shape `(*, M, N)`
3. Apply sigmoid gating: `output = sigmoid(g) * p`

The `dual_x` variant takes separate `x1` (for gating) and `x2` (for projection), enabling the output gating step in `triangle_multiplicative_update` where the gate is computed from normalized input and the projection from the contracted output [^12].

### Triton Autotuning

The GPU implementation uses Triton kernels with compile-time autotuning over tile sizes (`TILE_M`, `TILE_N`, `TILE_K`), pipeline stages, and warp counts. The autotuning system includes:

- **Config pruning**: Filters out configurations where tile dimensions don't divide the problem dimensions, avoiding launch-time failures [^13].
- **Cache key generation**: Inputs are hashed by shape, dtype, and precision to avoid redundant tuning for identical workloads [^14].
- **Decoy/benchmark helpers**: Validate configurations with dummy inputs before full benchmarking, gracefully handling shared memory limit errors [^15].

> [!TIP]
> The `CUEQ_TRITON_TUNING` environment variable controls autotuning strategy. Setting it to `"AOT"` enables ahead-of-time tuning at import time (slowest import, fastest runtime), `"ONDEMAND"` tunes on first use, and `None` (default) defers to Triton's built-in autotuner.

### Vmap-Compatible Batching

Both `sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm` and `layer_norm_transpose` support JAX's `vmap` through registered batching rules. The shared `naive_batching_rule` utility handles the general case: it fuses the vmap batch dimension with the primitive's native batch dimension, invokes the primitive once with the combined batch size, then unfuses the output dimensions — trading kernel launch overhead for a single larger invocation [^16].

Sources: [_sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm.py#L1086-L1098), [_sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm.py#L1142-L1154), [_sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm.py#L578-L660), [_sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm.py#L381-L462), [_naive_batching.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/_naive_batching.py#L20-L91)

## Triton-JAX Integration Layer

The `triton_utils` module provides the low-level bridge between JAX's XLA compiler and Triton GPU kernels. It is inspired by NVIDIA's TransformerEngine architecture and handles kernel compilation, PTX caching, dtype mapping, and MLIR lowering [^17].

The key abstraction is `triton_call`, a high-level function that wraps a Triton kernel callable into a JAX-compatible operation. It handles shape/dtype inference through abstract evaluation, GPU-specific lowering through `triton_call_lowering` (which generates MLIR call operations to compiled Triton kernels), and manages a kernel compilation cache keyed by compute capability, kernel hash, and compile parameters [^18].

Sources: [triton_utils.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/triton_utils.py#L16-L22), [triton_utils.py](cuequivariance_jax/cuequivariance_jax/triangle/triton_utils.py#L339-L373)

## Testing and Validation

The triangle subsystem maintains comprehensive test coverage across four test files, each validating a different layer of the stack [^19]:

| Test File | Scope | Key Tests |
|---|---|---|
| `triangle_attention_test.py` | Attention correctness | Gradient finite differences, dtype support (f32/f16/bf16), vmap batching, multi-head shapes |
| `triangle_multiplicative_update_test.py` | End-to-end TMU | PyTorch cross-implementation comparison, shape broadcasting, bias functionality, gradient accuracy, JIT compilation |
| `sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm_test.py` | Gated GEMM primitive | Manual computation verification, gradient correctness across backends, Triton autotuning modes, vmap forward/backward |
| `layer_norm_transpose_test.py` | Layer norm primitive | Layout permutation correctness, elementwise_affine toggle, vmap with fallback toggle |

The TMU tests explicitly compare JAX output against the PyTorch `cuequivariance_torch` implementation, establishing cross-framework numerical equivalence — a critical property for mixed-framework training pipelines [^20].

Sources: [triangle_attention_test.py](cuequivariance_jax/tests/triangle_attention_test.py#L68-L147), [triangle_multiplicative_update_test.py](cuequivariance_jax/tests/triangle_multiplicative_update_test.py#L66-L70), [sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm_test.py](cuequivariance_jax/tests/sigmoid_gated_dual_gemm_test.py#L197-L509), [layer_norm_transpose_test.py](cuequivariance_jax/tests/layer_norm_transpose_test.py#L25-L49)
